H1.text: Throw a paper ball into a bin. Kick a football. Spray water from a garden hose.

H2.text: Three different things, one same kind of curve.

H3.text: Aarav noticed it at his study table. He flicked a paper ball at the bin.

H4.text: It rose, turned, and dropped in one smooth curve. Is that curve a piece of a circle?

H5.text: By the end, you will know its exact shape, and prove it yourself.

P2.text: It is the path a projectile traces in the air. Every point on it is a pair of numbers, x and y.

P3.text: We already have two equations. One gives x at any time. One gives y.

P4.text: But a path does not care about time. To get its shape, we remove time, and write y using only x.

S1.text: Let's launch a ball in our motion notebook.

S2.text: It leaves at twenty metres per second, at forty five degrees.

S3.text: Across, the blue part never changes. So x grows in equal steps, in equal times.

S4.text: Up and down, the violet part shrinks, because gravity pulls down all the time.

S5.text: Slow motion at the top. The violet part is zero here. Only the blue part is left.

S6.text: On the graph, the dot draws y against x, as the ball flies.

D1.text: Now let's find its equation, one step at a time.

D2.text: Step one. Across, there is no acceleration. So x equals v naught cos theta, times t.

D3.text: Step two. Turn it around. Time t equals x, divided by v naught cos theta.

D4.text: Step three. Up and down, y equals v naught sin theta times t, minus half g t squared.

D5.text: Step four. Put this t from step two into step three.

D6.text: The first part becomes x tan theta. The second part becomes g x squared, over two v naught squared cos squared theta.

T1.text: Remember this. Remove time, and the path of a projectile is a parabola.

C1.text: Why a parabola? Look at the shape of the equation.

C2.text: For one throw, theta, v naught and g are fixed. So y equals a x, minus b x squared.

C3.text: The a x part alone is a straight line, along the launch direction.

C4.text: The minus b x squared part pulls it down, more as x grows. That is gravity. A line bent like this is a parabola.

K1.text: Side by side. With no gravity, b is zero. The ball flies in a straight line forever.

K2.text: With gravity, the line bends down. The far end drops the most, because the drop grows with x squared.

K3.text: Now you try. A ball rolls off a table, straight across. Is its path a parabola? Pause and decide.

K4.text: Yes! Theta is zero, so tan theta is zero. y equals minus g x squared, over two v naught squared. That is half a parabola.

B1.text: What changes the curve? Look at b.

B2.text: v naught squared sits at the bottom of b. Throw twice as fast, and b becomes four times smaller.

B3.text: So a faster throw bends more slowly. Its parabola is wider and taller.

B4.text: Your turn. Both leave at forty five degrees, one twice as fast. Ten metres across, which is higher? Pause and think.

B5.text: The faster one! Both start along the same line. But the faster ball has a smaller b, so it has dropped less.

W2.text: A ball is thrown at twenty metres per second, at forty five degrees. How high is it, ten metres across?

W3.text: At forty five degrees, tan theta is one, and cos squared theta is one half.

W4.text: So b equals nine point eight, over two times four hundred times one half. That is zero point zero two four five.

W5.text: Put x equals ten. y equals ten, minus zero point zero two four five times one hundred.

W6.text: y equals ten minus two point four five. The ball is seven point five five metres high.

X2.text: Many students write cos theta at the bottom, instead of cos squared theta.

X3.text: But t was squared, in half g t squared. So the whole t gets squared, and cos theta becomes cos squared theta.

E1.text: Where is this asked? You get a trajectory equation, and find the angle or the speed from it.

Q1.text: Exam level now. A projectile moves along y equals root three x, minus x squared over twenty. g is ten. Find the angle and the speed. Pause and solve.

A1.text: The answer is A. Sixty degrees, and twenty metres per second.

A2.text: Match it with y equals x tan theta. Tan theta is root three, so theta is sixty degrees.

A3.text: Next, g over two v naught squared cos squared theta equals one over twenty. Cos squared sixty is one quarter, so v naught squared is four hundred, and v naught is twenty.

F1.text: Here is your recap. Screenshot this card.

Y1.text: Can you answer these three questions without help?

Y2.text: One. Why do we remove time to find the shape of the path?

Y3.text: Two. In the trajectory equation, why is cos theta squared?

Y4.text: Three. What would the path be if there were no gravity?

N1.text: Next time: same speed, thirty degrees or sixty. Which stays in the air longer? Find out in time of flight.
